scores.name: Body motion
scores.note: FlowHMR on court-level footage, accepted across 16 points. Judged on how it looks and times, not measured depth: FlowHMR reports 82.47% physical tracking success on Wild-4K (GVHMR 62.82%) and about 57 mm world-aligned joint error on the RICH benchmark.

scores.name: Ball
scores.note: Ball found in frame and estimated arcs, 30 fps; hidden where unsupported. Not spin or measured 3D flight. RacketVision's tennis ball tracker reports recall 0.880.

scores.name: Racket model design
scores.note: A craft judgement: traced outline, woven strings, drilled grommets; depth and sidewalls approximate.

scores.name: Racket motion
scores.note: Solved through the arm; face at contact set by rule, not measured. Generous at 30 fps, where the racket is found in only 32 to 40% of frames; fair at 120 fps (81%). RacketVision reaches 89.6% correct keypoints on broadcast clips, with the side points weakest at about 80%.

scores.name: Skin and face texture, Meshy
scores.note: Fair for outfit and surface, not face: heads were rejected and hands came out as mittens, which Meshy's own help page lists as known limits.

scores.name: Body shape specific to the person
scores.note: A pipeline choice: every player shares the FlowHMR body; Rodin bodies are paused.

scores.name: Skin and face texture, FlowHMR with a rig
Face likeness
scores.note: Rodin, UP2You and Meshy all generated a face; none is a likeness, and neither vendor promises one from two or three photos.

scores_note: Self-assessed. Scores judge the viewing result, not a measured match to the player. Frame rate matters most for the racket and ball. The gold standard is Hawk-Eye SkeleTRACK: 29 body points and 7 racket points from a stadium camera system, not one YouTube camera. Numbers next to a score come from the cited paper, measured on its own benchmarks, not on this footage.

groups.title: Other cameras and frame rates
groups.note: Same FlowHMR, different footage. This is where quality changes.

back.source: Slow-Mo Tennis · Indian Wells 2023 practice, 4K 120 fps
back.ran: FlowHMR at 30 fps upsampled to 120; RacketVision on every 120 fps frame; racket solved through the arm; contact rule at frame 650.
back.why: Best racket result of the whole project: the detector keeps the racket through contact and follow-through. 15.5 px median on held-out frames.
back.differs: Only clip at 120 fps. Everything else is 30 fps, where the racket blurs at contact and the detector loses it.
back.cost: inside the RacketVision batch, about $0.40 Modal

back.source: Court Level Tennis · Indian Wells practice, high diagonal seat
back.ran: 4K master matched to the 720p clip frame for frame, cropped to 1080p; FlowHMR on the crop; RacketVision on 4K and 720p merged; 11 backhand frames hand-marked.
back.why: Body fit improved from 8.6 to 6.9 px. The racket detector got worse on 4K (151 confident frames vs 181 on 720p). Forehand contacts are edge-on and stay unmarked.
back.differs: Camera is high and diagonal with a coach and partner in frame; player only about 260 px tall in the 720p clip. This camera is the ceiling for groundstrokes.

back.ran: FlowHMR only, same fixed Shelton body as the court-level serve. No racket, ball or opponent solved.
back.why: Full-court view explains play, but the player is about 220 px tall so the wrist and face carry no usable detail. Kept as a benchmark, not a demo.
back.differs: Output is a live 3D scene on the Tennis Lab site, not a four-up video: the four-up export was built later for the rear-court recipe and was not run on this clip.

back.source: Manufacturer photos traced for the outline; string axes and grommet positions authored
back.ran: build_racket.py in Blender, then material and finish passes, then an export gate that re-imports the GLB and checks every string passage.
back.why: Depth and sidewalls are approximate, not CAD. Texture artwork was authored from references, not scanned.

items.title: Racket solved through the arm
items.sub: Red old fit, green arm solve, cyan detections

back.ran: Instead of placing the racket freely at the wrist, solve forearm twist and wrist angle per frame inside anatomical limits, smooth over time, cap spin.
back.why: A racket seen from behind looks the same rotated 180 degrees about its handle, so the free fit flipped the face between frames (up to 5,400°/s). After: no frame over 2,600°/s on 15 of 16 points.

items.title: Face angle at contact
items.sub: Before and after the contact rule

back.source: All 16 library points plus the 120 fps forehand
back.ran: Contact frame and shot type labelled by eye for every clear swing; for ±3 frames the face is held vertical to 15° closed (topspin) or 15° closed to 10° open (serve).
back.why: From behind, open and closed faces shrink the string outline by the same amount, so five points cannot tell them apart. The rule chose the angle, not the video; the true angle is inside the range, not measured.

back.ran: RacketVision on every 120 fps frame, fit through the arm.
back.why: Frames 613 to 622 (the lag before contact) have no detection and the fill is about 45° off. Frame 664 has a false detection on the head.

back.ran: One hand-to-handle registration per stroke family, separated from forearm roll and wrist motion.
back.why: Grip rotation and contact depth remain inferred. No evidence for axial sliding during a swing, so it stays zero.

back.ran: RacketVision on a T4 over all rear-court clips plus the 120 fps source.
back.why: Five racket points per frame where visible: 32 to 81 percent of frames depending on frame rate. Availability is not accuracy.
